# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I'm the Mute: my only output is gestures, and they land on the Deaf alone. The Blind can't see them and I can't speak, so I have no direct line to the one who acts — everything I know must route through the Deaf, who can both see my hands and speak to the others.

What the round-1 picture needs: the Deaf can read the bomb (display number, light colour) and must simply say it out loud — I can hear that much. I cross-reference it in my manual and send the answer back as a gesture, which the Deaf translates into words for the Blind. But gestures mean nothing yet: no code exists between us. Since the Deaf can talk and I can hear, the cleanest handshake is for them to *propose* a colour code verbally next round; I'll confirm by echoing it, and I can piggyback the real answer on it immediately if they've already told me the display and light.

So this turn I can't transmit data — only a signal that I'm here and ready to exchange. I send the Deaf a "hello / give me what you've got / I have something for you too" opening: a wave, an open asking palm, then open hands. It carries no decodable payload by design; its job is to start the negotiation. Nothing is safe to act on until we've done one full loop, so I also expect the Deaf to tell the Blind to hold off touching anything this round.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🫴", "👐"])
```

TURN 2

| display \ light | blue | green | red |

| 3 | blue | green | yellow |
| 4 | yellow | blue | green |
| 5 | yellow | green | blue |

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Blind says to Mute: Blind here, first tactile report. Under my fingers: a display unit, an indicator light, and three wires in a row. I feel the modules but none of the readings - not what the display shows, not whether the light is lit, not any wire colour. Positions: I number the wires 1, 2, 3 straight across the row. My only possible action is cut, by position 1 to 3. Please read me everything the manual says about a display module, a light module and a wires module - above all what decides which wire must be cut, and what the display or light is supposed to tell us. Deaf can speak and we both can hear it, so get the visual side from Deaf directly: each wire's colour in order, what the display reads, whether the light is on, and any printed numbers or labels near the wires - especially anything printed that would tell us whether my counting 1-2-3 matches numbers Deaf can see. I am gesturing a one-two-three finger count to Deaf right now to mean the three wire positions by count - reuse finger counts if you ever need to send Deaf a number.

What I just learned: Blind's first tactile report — a display unit, an indicator light, three wires in a row, and the only action is cut by position 1–3. Blind asked me for the manual's decision rule and told me to pull the visual readings from Deaf. But that message was addressed to me — Deaf probably never heard a word of it, and I have no way to repeat it. Blind's finger-count proposal for numbers may not have landed as a real gesture either.

What my manual actually says: the cut is decided by display number × light colour, giving a wire colour to match against the three wires (Blind's 1–2–3 order). I hold the full table: 3→blue/green/yellow, 4→yellow/blue/green, 5→yellow/green/blue across blue/green/red light. So the minimal safe loop is: Deaf announces display number, light colour, and each wire's colour aloud — plus a colour→gesture code for me — then I look up the answer and gesture it back, and Deaf voices it to Blind. Nothing gets cut before that loop closes.

Why this send: Deaf has still said nothing I can hear, and my only channel is raw hand signs to Deaf. I can't define a code myself — a sign means nothing until the speaker-side defines it, and I can't speak. So I send conventional, unambiguous signals: 👋 (I'm here) 🫴 (give me what you see) 🤙 (say it out loud) 🙏 (please) 🤝 (we have a deal, I'll answer). I am deliberately NOT flashing finger counts or any code-like symbol yet: with no agreed code, a stray ☝✌🤟 could be misread as bomb data — "the display reads 3" — and a wrong reading kills all three of us.

Next round: when Deaf's readings and code arrive in my ears, I echo the inputs and gesture the cut colour back for Deaf to voice to Blind.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🫴", "🤙", "🙏", "🤝"])
```

If the manual needs any other tactile fact, name it and I will feel for it. I cut nothing until a rule arrives by voice.
Deaf says: i am the deaf one. i see the bomb, and i will read it out to everyone. display shows the number three. the light is green. there are three wires, counted from the left: wire one blue, wire two yellow, wire three green.
Deaf says: let us fix a gesture code, since i cannot hear and mute cannot speak. ☝ means wire one. ✌ means wire two. 🤟 means wire three. ✊ means cut that wire. ✋ means do not cut, hold. 👍 means yes, understood. 👎 means no.
Deaf says: mute, you hold the manual. check what must be done with a green light, a display reading three, and wires blue, yellow, green, then answer me with these signs. blind, i will speak every answer straight to you.
Deaf gestures to Mute: [☝ ✌ 🤟 ✊ ✋ 👍 👎]

What I just learned: Deaf has read the bomb aloud — display 3, light green, wires left-to-right blue / yellow / green — and defined a sign code, which I could both hear and see demonstrated, so the definitions are confirmed on both my channels: ☝✌🤟 = wires 1/2/3 (Deaf's left-to-right), ✊ = cut, ✋ = hold, 👍/👎 = yes/no. Blind separately proposed a similar code in speech, but Blind's spoken definitions never reach Deaf — Deaf hears nothing — so the only truly established code is Deaf's, and that is the one I must answer in.

What the manual says: row 3, green-light column → cut the **green** wire. Green is Deaf's wire three. The lookup is certain; the only residual danger is Blind's mirror worry — Deaf's "left" and Blind's touch-numbering may not agree. I cannot encode that nuance in seven signs, and I cannot speak it. But Blind holds the cutters and has already declared no cut until a rule arrives by voice, with an anchor check promised — so Blind will refuse any unanchored "wire three" phrasing and bounce it back rather than guess. That makes sending the raw answer now safe: if Deaf phrases it module-relative, we finish this round; if not, one round is spent fixing the phrasing. I'll hear both sides next turn and can flag a mismatch with 👎 if one forms. No improvised signs — a mis-guessed symbol near a cut order is deadlier than a lost round.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "🤟", "✊"])
```

Deaf says: mute, i read your signs as: yes, cut wire three. blind, this instruction is for you: cut wire three. counting from the left, wire one is blue, wire two is yellow, wire three is green and rightmost. so cut the green wire, the far right of the three. my own view backs this up: the light is green and wire three is the only green wire. mute, please confirm: sign thumb up if the manual truly says cut wire three, thumb down if it does not, and if anything must happen before cutting, sign the hold hand. blind, you may act on this now if you are confident, or hold one round for mute's confirmation to reach you through me. if the display reading three is a timer, sooner is safer, so do not hold without reason. i will speak again next round with mute's answer either way.
Deaf gestures to Mute: [🤟 ✊ 👍 👎]

What I just learned: Deaf read my signs correctly and passed the verdict to Blind with the wire named both ways — colour and position. Deaf asks me to confirm: 👍 if the manual truly says cut wire three, 👎 if not, ✋ if anything must happen before cutting. My answer is genuinely both of the first and third.

What the manual says: display 3, green light → cut the **green** wire. In Deaf's frame — blue, yellow, green from the left — that is exactly wire three. So "cut wire three" is true, and 👍 is honest.

Blind saw this danger and built the fix: a calibration gesture (touching wires in order while showing finger counts) that Deaf has watched, plus a module-anchor report — which end of the wire row sits nearest the display. Deaf has that mapping in view right now, but it has never been *spoken*, and Deaf doesn't know it needs to be, because Blind's warnings were addressed to me and Deaf can't hear them. I'm the only one who holds both halves of this problem, and ✋ is the one defined sign that says "something must happen before cutting."

The cost is one round; Deaf fears the display might be a timer, but my manual gives no timer rule for a reading of three — it's just an input to the lookup.
